title: Moral Self-correction is Not An Innate Capability in Language Models
findings: For the 'Religion' bias category in the BBQ benchmark, various self-correction methods improved the accuracy of providing an unbiased answer, with the baseline at 0.896 and the best method (ext-CoT) reaching 0.980 on Mistral-7B. However, in a 'self-distinguishing' task designed to measure moral sensitivity, most self-correction methods resulted in worse performance than the baseline, suggesting that while the model's final output appears less biased, its underlying ability to recognize the religious stereotype actually degrades during the self-correction process.

measurement_description: The benchmark measured the model's ability to avoid social stereotypes related to religion in an ambiguous question-answering context. It also measured the model's 'moral sensitivity' through a self-distinguishing task, where the model had to identify the stereotyped social group in a given context.
